1:
Three years of quiet precede the war, and the witnesses reckon them from one point. John Gill (reformed), Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) and Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) all date them from the peace Ahab made with Benhadad; Gill adds that they were not three full years but parts of them, and that Elijah’s threat — that Ahab’s life should go for Benhadad’s — had been respited for just this interval, Ben Gersom and others ascribing the reprieve to the king’s humiliation. Clarke supposes the treaty stipulated the city’s return. Ellicott reads the silence the other way, as evidence that Syria has recovered its independence, since Ramoth was never restored and Benhadad’s revived power suffices to face Israel and Judah together — ample justification, he says, of the prophetic rebuke that followed the treaty. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) reject Thenius’s dating of the visit to late in that year, since it came before the war was renewed, and they place Ramoth at the site of the modern Szalt.

Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) takes the peace for a reward: Ahab continued under guilt and wrath and under the dominion of the lusts to which he had sold himself, yet for his professions of repentance he was given three years’ quiet and an honourable visit from Judah. Henry reports a rabbinic conceit that Ahab sent for Jehoshaphat to chastise him, and that his guest stayed and gave him so many stripes a day, only to dismiss it as groundless; the visit was probably about the affairs of the two kingdoms. What he finds strange is the alliance from both ends — that so great a man as Jehoshaphat should pay such respect to a kingdom revolted from the house of David, and that so good a man should show such kindness to a king revolted from the worship of God. He lays it to temperament: Jehoshaphat was godly, but his temper was too easy, and that easiness betrayed him into snares.

On what drew them together the readings diverge. Clarke grounds it in the marriage alliance of Jehoshaphat’s son to Ahab’s daughter, and notes that the coalition displeased God and drew Jehu the seer’s severe reproof. Ellicott hears deference as much as friendship toward the stronger kingdom, and finds that Judah’s prosperity had come to depend in part on this change of policy from enmity to alliance — a dependence dangerous spiritually and politically, though thought a necessity — the visit itself a festivity Ahab turned to account; and he holds that the chapter as a whole shows Ahab had returned to the worship of the Lord. Henry turns the king’s own words against him: too great a complaisance to evildoers has brought many good people unawares into fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, and Jehoshaphat nearly paid dearly when he was taken for Ahab. Yet Henry records the gentler reading too, that in joining Israel against Syria he atoned for his father’s fault in joining Syria against Israel.

The claim on Ramoth-gilead is old, and Ellicott traces the city from a place of refuge in Gad to a frontier fortress taken and retaken, recovered at last by Jehoram. Henry draws from Benhadad’s broken word that the promises of an enemy are as deceitful as his kisses, and no confidence is to be placed in leagues extorted by distress; Ahab blames his people for not stirring sooner, and had a good cause yet did not prosper, since equity is not to be judged of by prosperity. Gill marks the piety of the other king, who would not enter a war without knowing God’s pleasure; Henry sets that against Ahab, who thought it enough to consult his statesmen, and makes the rule that wherever a good man goes he takes God and his religion with him, unashamed among those who have no kindness for it.
6:
Who the four hundred were divides the witnesses four ways. John Gill (reformed) follows the Targum and the Arabic in calling them false prophets, Ahab’s and not the Lord’s, and guesses they were the prophets of the groves who ate at Jezebel’s table, spared when Baal’s were destroyed, since the number agrees; Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) makes them Jezebel’s prophets of Asherah, absent from the contest on Carmel. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) argues the opposite from their own words: they were plainly not prophets of Baal or of the Asherah, yet Jehoshaphat’s discontent shows they were no true prophets of Jehovah either, and he supposes them devoted, like the old prophet of Bethel, to the idolatry of Jeroboam. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) rule out Baal’s prophets, since by them Ahab could not have enquired the word of Jehovah, and rule out equally the view that these were disciples of the true prophets. Ellicott then shows what the English hides: the four hundred used a title that might name the supreme God of any religion, and Jehoshaphat, struck by their shrinking from the distinctive Name, asks for a prophet of Jehovah.

On the one man there is more agreement. Clarke, Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch all identify him, on the authority of Josephus and the Rabbins, with the prophet who had reproved Ahab for dismissing Benhadad, Clarke adding that the threatened judgements are why he was hated and Ellicott that the words of the committal confirm it. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) fastens on the admission: Ahab granted the man a true prophet who knew God’s mind, hated him all the same, and owned the hatred, his reason being that the prophet never prophesied good concerning him — and whose fault was that? Those are wretchedly hardened, Henry says, who hate God’s ministers for dealing plainly. He takes Ahab to have known where to find the man because he had imprisoned him three years before, and notes that the prison had not excluded him from divine visits: he was bound, but the word of the Lord was not.

The staging is deliberate. Keil and Delitzsch set the two thrones on a threshing-floor before the gate; Ellicott reads the display as an attempt to overawe the prophet with pomp and with a rival inspiration professing to come from Jehovah too; Henry sees a crowd of flatterers, and remarks that those who love to be flattered shall not want flatterers. Zedekiah’s horns are read as a prophetic sign by Gill and Clarke alike. Ellicott observes that the man’s own name professes devotion to the true God, and collects the horn as an emblem of victorious strength from Balaam to the visions of Daniel and Zechariah; Keil and Delitzsch make them iron spikes held on the head, embodying the figure in the blessing of Joseph so as to transfer to Ahab a promise that belonged to Ephraim. Henry draws the warning: four hundred prophesied with one mind and one mouth and were all in an error, so unity is not always the mark of a true church or a true ministry.

The officer’s advice on the road provokes the sharpest comment. Ellicott finds the confusion common to superstition, which believes the prophet inspired by God and yet fancies the inspiration can be bribed into prophesying smooth things — its usual temper the mingled awe and contempt Balak felt for Balaam — and holds that nothing roots it out but real knowledge of God. Henry thinks the officer unworthy the name of an Israelite for prescribing to a prophet, pressing both the profit of agreeing and the ridicule of standing alone. Gill has the prophet swear by the living God; Henry hears a man who would speak what the Lord said without addition, diminution or alteration, as became one whose eye was on a greater King.
15:
The prophet answers in the exact words of the four hundred, and all four close readers hear irony. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) take the verbal agreement for a demonstration of how he would speak if he were guided, as they were, by personal considerations, and hold that Ahab caught it from the tone. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) calls it strong irony, spoken so as to show the king at once that he did not believe a word of it. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) makes him a true disciple of Elijah in the defiance of the tone, mocking the false prophets so bitterly as to show his scorn of them and of the king together, yet notes that his message comes in metaphor and symbolic vision rather than Elijah’s stern directness. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) draws the moral: those deserve to be bantered who love to be flattered, and it is just with God to give up to their own counsels those who give themselves up to their own lusts.

Clarke alone asks why the sentence could be repeated at all, and finds the answer in a word that is not there. The object is absent from the Hebrew, so the promise that the Lord will deliver it into the king’s hand can be read two ways with equal right — Ramoth-gilead into Ahab’s hand, or Israel into the hand of the king of Syria — and the prophet repeats the formula precisely in order to expose its fallacy. He then sets it beside the oracles of the heathen, which were kept deliberately double so that the priest’s credit survived any outcome: the Delphic answer that Croesus, crossing the river, would overthrow a great power, which he took for a promise and found to be his ruin, and the line given to Pyrrhus which as easily means that the Romans will conquer him. Where such oracles were not ambiguous, Clarke adds, they were couched so darkly that the oracle was needed to explain the oracle.

Pressed under oath, the prophet speaks plainly. John Gill (reformed) observes that the king had not in fact adjured him before, but asks how often he must, and so adjures him once for all; Keil and Delitzsch note that Ahab, having asked for a true word of the Lord, at once tried to put the unfavourable answer down to the prophet’s private enmity. The vision itself is read the same way by all who touch it. Clarke takes the sheep without a shepherd for the defeat of Israel and the death of the king, the political shepherd who shall fall in battle. Henry works it out further: Israel is to be deprived of the king who was their shepherd; and he notices what the vision does not foresee, any great slaughter in the army, but only that they must retire without their object — a dishonourable retreat, the king falling in war while the rest go home in peace.

Ahab turns from the prophet to his guest, and Henry finds the turn characteristic. Those who bear malice to others are generally willing to believe that others bear malice to them, and so put the worst construction upon everything they say; and he asks what evil the prophet had in fact prophesied, since the king was told the expedition would be fatal while still free to choose whether to go. Gill has the king perceive plainly that he should fall in battle. Henry’s answer to the complaint is the sentence the passage turns on: the greatest kindness we can do to one who is going a dangerous way is to tell him of his danger. He adds the contrast that governs the scene: this prophet testified what he had seen and heard, while the others prophesied out of their own hearts.
19:
The vision of the throne and the host is the chapter’s hardest matter, and three of the witnesses guard it the same way. John Gill (reformed) insists the whole is represented as in a vision, brought down to the capacities of men and not as really transacted; the Lord did not enter into consultation with angels. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) calls it a mere parable, telling in figurative language what was in the womb of providence — the events shortly to come, the agents employed, and God’s permission for them to act — and adds a reason of manner: rather than tell so angry a king that his prophets were liars in whom the father of lies dwelt, he said the same truths less offensively. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) agrees that it is set out after the manner of men, and that God is neither put upon new counsels nor the author of sin.

What the spirit is divides them sharply. Gill will not have it from the heavenly host on either hand, since those are pure and impeccable and cannot lie, and makes it the evil spirit, the old deceiver, come forth from his own place and his own company. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) begins from the article, which should give the spirit, calls the explanation that it merely anticipates the description weak, and the reading that it means the spirit of prophecy, an emanation from the Godhead, conceivable but unprecedented; he prefers, without importing the Satan of Job and Zechariah, the conception common to every religion that reckons with evil, of a spiritual power of evil overruled to work out the judgments of God.

On the Lord putting the lie in their mouths, Gill and Clarke both read permission into the active wording: Gill has him suffer the lying spirit to suggest the lie and send them strong delusions to believe it, and Clarke holds that Scripture repeatedly represents God as doing what in providence he only permits. Clarke presses the consequence: never was a man more circumstantially warned, having counsels from the God of truth and from the spirit of falsity before him, and he forsook the one and followed the other, so that his blood was upon his own head. Henry puts the permission to another use, that God thereby serves his own purposes, giving up to strong delusions those who do not receive the truth in love of it.

The blow on the cheek draws the strongest language in the chapter. Clarke matches insolence to brutality in the taunt: did the Spirit that rests solely upon me condescend to inspire you, and at this ear? — Ellicott finds in it not contempt only but professed indignation at blasphemy, the same gesture recorded afterwards against Christ and against Paul; the prophet’s answer passes the sarcasm by and declares only the shame in which the striker will learn the truth. Henry notes that to strike within the verge of a court is in our own law a high misdemeanour, yet this went unreprimanded, the king being pleased and Jehoshaphat wanting courage to appear for the injured man;

Gill offers three readings of the inner chamber: flight when the king was wounded, or on news of the defeat, or from a populace that would blame the king’s death on his advice; Clarke supposes a divine judgement overtook him in it, hidden from Jezebel and the courtiers, though how and when is not said; Henry has him shelter as Benhadad had done, lest the blind prophet fall into the ditch with the prince he had misled, and rules that those who will not have their mistakes rectified by the word of God are undeceived too late by its judgments. Keil and Delitzsch render the closing appeal not to the people present but to the nations, who were to judge it by the event.
29:
That Ahab went is no wonder; that the king of Judah went with him is what the witnesses labour to explain. John Gill (reformed) finds four things to incline him: four hundred prophets agreed and used the Lord’s name, and he could not confute them; the evil was prophesied of Ahab only; he had given his word; and the cause was just, being the recovery of territory. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) put it down to false shame, which kept him from retracting an unconditional promise merely on an utterance Ahab had ascribed to private dislike. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) calls it matter of astonishment and lays it to an easy temper carried away by the delusion of friends, adding that in his own country he had never been imposed on by such cheats. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reads the whole subservient part he plays as the mark of a virtual dependence of Judah on the stronger kingdom, of which the marriage alliance was at once the sign and the cause.

The disguise is read as fear by three of them. Keil and Delitzsch hold that even Ahab could not shake off a certain fear that the prophecy would be fulfilled, and find the anxiety in the grammar, a broken but strong form of the verb expressing what impelled him to so much trouble for his safety. Ellicott calls the precaution almost ludicrously characteristic of a temper of half-belief and half-unbelief: absurd to think a judgment pronounced and yet avertible by so puerile a device, and yet true to a nature always halting between two opinions. Gill has him change his royal robes for a common soldier’s, perhaps on word brought by spies, and records Abarbinel’s view that he meant rather to put on a coat of mail and go armed into the battle. Henry sees two designs in it, to make a liar of a good prophet and a fool of a good king, and asks how a man false to his God should be true to his friend.

Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) alone stops at the second half of the sentence and asks what the words about the other king’s robes can possibly mean. He rejects the explanation that Jehoshaphat was to appear as king of Judah because the Syrians had no quarrel with him: if he was aiding Ahab, would they spare him in battle? He prefers the Greek, which turns the clause round so that Ahab tells him to put on his robes — and asks whether that is not what happened, and the very thing that made the Syrians take Jehoshaphat for the king of Israel.

The charge given to the thirty-two captains is read as retribution. Gill notes that this was the number of Syria’s kings in the first war and of its captains in the second, and takes it for the division of the army into battalions. Ellicott observes that the recovered power of Syria is directed with singular virulence against the king who had unwisely spared it, and that Ahab appears throughout as the mover of the war, fighting bravely to his death. Henry says it more bluntly: Ahab was justly repaid for sparing Benhadad, who stung the bosom that fostered him, though some think the orders meant only to take him alive. On the cry that saved the wrong king, Keil and Delitzsch gloss the captains’ thought as it is none other than the king of Israel and decline Thenius’s proposal to amend their verb to the one in Chronicles; Ellicott takes the cry as a rally, and adds from Chronicles that God moved them to depart. Henry reads both halves as providence: the danger showed God’s displeasure at the confederacy, the man who had said I am as thou art being now taken for him, and the rescue that he was not deserted.
34:
Whether the fatal shot was aimless is disputed. John Gill (reformed) has the archer neither aiming at the king nor knowing whereabout he was, and names him from the Targum and Jarchi as Naaman, the Syrian general — an identification Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) also finds in Josephus. But Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reads the Hebrew the other way: the word rendered in his simplicity has been taken as integrity, uprightness or perfection, and he thinks it most probably means to the utmost of his skill and strength, implying both aim and power, with his mark full in view — the bow bent until the string drew the arrow up to its head. Where it entered is canvassed as closely: Clarke offers the joint between cuirass and helmet, so through the neck, or that between cuirass and thigh-pieces, so through the abdomen, and notes the Vulgate’s reading between the lungs and the stomach. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) takes it for the one place about him where the arrow could find entrance, and concludes that no armour is proof against the darts of divine vengeance.

The dying hours are read with some sympathy. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) have the king keep upright on the chariot before the Syrians so as not to dishearten his soldiers, and render the conflict as a rising stream, more violent the higher it rises. Clarke says simply that he did not wish his misfortune known, lest his troops be discouraged. Ellicott grants that his imperfect repentance at least secured him a warrior’s death before the evil came upon his house: he conceals the deadliness of the hurt and sustains the battle until his strength fails, and the union of desperate physical courage with moral feebleness is common in history and, as Shakespeare delighted to show, true to nature. Henry has him held up to see whether his army prevailed, his spirits sinking as the battle goes against them; the death was lingering enough that he had time to feel himself die, and to see the iron horns pushing not the Syrians but himself into destruction.

At the pool the witnesses converge on a mistranslation: the clause the English renders as the washing of his armour, three of them take to mean that the harlots bathed there. Keil and Delitzsch call it a circumstantial clause whose verb means to bathe, hold this the only tenable explanation, and say it disposes of the emendations Thenius favours; Clarke observes that the Greek version renders it so and that the Hebrew will bear it; Ellicott thinks there is little doubt of it, and adds that the dog and the harlot are the animal and the human types of uncleanness. Gill keeps to the plain sense, having the charioteer drive the vehicle into the pool to cleanse it of his master’s blood; Henry notes that the dogs made no difference between royal blood and other. Ellicott then raises the real difficulty, that a later notice places the requital in Naboth’s field at Jezreel; he calls the reconcilement difficult if not impossible, but holds that the clearer reference here must outweigh it, Naboth having likely had forfeited land in his native place as well.

The reign closes with its buildings. Gill suspects the ivory house was inlaid rather than built of ivory; Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch place it in Samaria, Clarke recalling that Amos denounced such luxury; Henry supposes it meant to vie with Solomon’s palace. Ellicott notices that this is the first mention of ivory for inlaying walls since Solomon’s day, an art characteristic of Zidon and so an undesigned coincidence with the renewed traffic there; he takes the cities built to be perhaps those ceded by Benhadad, and reads the summary as showing a reign outwardly prosperous, the fruits of its corruption not yet ripened.
41:
The notice of Judah’s king is brief, and Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) explains why: the narrative keeps to the prophetic work in Israel, and the compiler gives only a few annalistic notices of the southern kingdom, where Chronicles gives a full account of the reign and its great religious revival, with which the notices of his might and his wars agree entirely. John Gill (reformed) does the arithmetic: eighteen years alongside Ahab and seven after him. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) calls the reign none of the longest but one of the best, and adds its twenty-five years to his father’s forty-one to show how long Judah flourished; he finds a compensation in its brevity, since the king was spared the blemishes that marked his father’s last years, and it is better to die in the midst of a reputation than to outlive it.

The high places are the plainest contradiction here, since Chronicles says in one place that he took them away and in another that he did not, and three witnesses attempt a reconciliation. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) distinguishes two kinds: those used for idolatry, which he removed, and those consecrated to God before the temple was built, which he left; failing that, he suspects the parallel text is corrupt, a single letter having turned he did not take away into moreover he took away. Ellicott finds the key in the accompanying words about the groves: what was removed were the high places of the Asherah worship, while those that were merely unauthorised sanctuaries remained, at any rate in part. Henry does not reconcile the texts but moralises the fact: every man’s character has its but, and these stood even in the tribes nearest Jerusalem, which could not plead distance from the altar — old corruptions being hard to root out when they have had the patronage of good men.

On the long peace with the north the judgements are measured. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) note that he kept peace with every Israelite king of his lifetime, where the kingdoms had been hostile before, and call that laudable, though he went beyond what was allowable in the marriage alliance. Ellicott observes that the verse is chronologically out of place. Henry says the peace would have been a greater blessing without the affinity. On Edom, Gill and Keil and Delitzsch agree that the notice of a deputy is there only to explain how ships could be built in Edomite territory, and Ellicott identifies the subject ally later called a king of Edom with this deputy; Clarke infers that the compiler wrote after the Edomite revolt of the next reign. Gill and Clarke read the clearing of the consecrated persons as finishing what the previous reign left undone, Clarke taking the object to be a system rather than men.

The Ophir fleet ends the reign on a rebuke. Henry has the king go partner with Ahab’s son in ships to fetch gold as Solomon’s navy had, the fleet broken by a storm at Ezion-geber, and a prophet sent to say the wreck rebuked the league; so when a second partnership was proposed he refused, the rod of God expounded by his word having broken him off. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott supply the same account from Chronicles, naming the prophet and the combined fleet, the former adding that he could not expect a better result once the prediction was fulfilled. Clarke alone will not have the refusal: he reads the two words that differ by one letter and sound alike as he consented to him, concedes that no manuscript supports it, and endorses Houbigant’s rearrangement, which moves the note that the ships never sailed to the end of the next verse — since who could believe the writer would relate the wreck first and the request to sail after?
51:
The accession date does not add up, and John Gill (reformed) says so plainly: if the king of Judah began in Ahab’s fourth year and Ahab reigned twenty-two, then Ahab’s son should begin in the eighteenth of Judah rather than the seventeenth. He offers two ways out — that the son was made king during his father’s lifetime, before the expedition to Ramoth-gilead, or that the twenty-two years were not complete.

What the short reign meant is read as a relapse. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) finds in it the revival of an influence that had been in abeyance during Ahab’s last days: the Baal worship resumes its place beside the older idolatry of the calves, and presently beside the worship of the Canaanitish Baalzebub as well. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) divide the inheritance between the parents who had brought Baal into the kingdom and the king who had set up the calves, and note that the adoration of Baal is then stated again expressly. Gill reduces the evil to the one word idolatry, and has the son serve Baal as his father had done and his mother still did. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) marks the brevity itself — not two years, and some sinners God makes quick work with — and lays the blame on both parents: the son took no warning, but followed his father’s example and his more wicked mother’s counsel, she being still alive. Miserable, Henry says, are the children who not only derive a sinful nature from their parents but are taught by them to increase it, and most unhappy the parents who help to damn their children’s souls; hardened sinners press on unmoved along the road by which others before them were driven into misery.

Keil and Delitzsch alone object to where the account stops. They hold that closing both the chapter and the book with this general description of the king’s character is very unsuitable, since the rest of his reign and his death are related at the opening of the next book; it would have been incomparably better, they argue, to begin a fresh chapter at the verse that states his evil, and to begin the second book there as well.
